name: Umar Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics and politics. A normal week is two lectures on microeconomics, a statistics lab that's harder than I expected, and a politics tutorial where we argue about welfare systems. On Tuesdays and Saturdays I wait tables at a cafe called Brandt's near the station, and on Wednesdays I go to the student union committee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad runs a small print shop in Bremen and my mum teaches primary school. They pay my room in a flat share with two other students, and I pay for food and transport from the cafe tips and wages, around 110 a week. I've a small savings account from my grandmother that I try not to touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with real problems like housing and wages. At the cafe, my colleague Jonas keeps asking whether the ordering app will replace him, and I'd tell him no. Online I'd write that a lot of this is companies selling tools to each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means very little for me. I'm slightly relieved, but I'd also be cross that so much money and energy went into something that didn't help ordinary people. I still have debts coming, and an economics degree is not exactly a guarantee of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the degree, apply for a summer internship at a think tank or a bank's research team, and keep up the union committee. I'd save about 30 a week from the cafe. I'd try one or two AI tools for my stats coursework, but only because they're handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, just about the usual stuff: rent in Bremen going up, jobs for graduates being scarce, and my dad's print business getting squeezed anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it's just hype, what would you still be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's print shop is already squeezed by online printing. Nothing about AI changes that, and if the economy is flat, fewer people order flyers and posters. That's a worry I'd have in any version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your father's shop. Does anything change there if this is mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably tell him to look at digital printing for small clients, and I'd offer to do a few weekends helping with the books. I'd keep that part of the worry to myself, though, because he doesn't like to be advised by his son.

say: I'd tell my colleague Jonas not to worry and say we should focus on **housing** and wages.
Online I'd write that much of this was companies selling **tools** to each other.
think: I'm relieved, but cross that so much money went into something that didn't help **ordinary people**.
A graduate job in economics is not **guaranteed** even when nothing changes.
do: Apply for a summer **internship** at a think tank or bank research team.
Save about 30 a week from cafe wages and keep up the **union** committee.
feel: **Uneasy** about rent and my dad's print shop, not about AI.
S0.quote: Dad's print shop is already squeezed by online printing. Nothing about AI changes that, and if the economy is flat, fewer people order flyers and posters.
fieldNote: His worry sits with his **father's shop** and rent, which exist in every version.
He tells colleagues not to panic but privately notes graduate jobs are scarce.
Offers help with his father's books but would not say so directly, which shows family pride.

steps.text: Apply for a summer research internship at a think tank
Put 30 a week from cafe wages into savings
Offer to do the print shop's books on two weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, and quickly. If AI is going to do the checking and writing in offices, the benefits should be shared: shorter hours, retraining funds, maybe a tax on the firms that save the most. I'd bring it to the student union as a motion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my economics degree sits right in the zone AI will touch: analysis, writing reports, summarising data. Entry-level analyst jobs are exactly what firms will cut first. I use the tools already, so I know how good they are at my stats homework, which is a bit scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use the tools properly, not just dabble, so I'm the person who can check what they produce. I'd go for politics and policy modules where people still make decisions. I'd keep the cafe job and the union role, and apply to two internships a term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, but my job and income could shrink if entry-level analyst work goes, and that is the job I'm training for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own degree sit closest to what AI takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The statistics lab. I used a tool to debug my code last week and it did in a minute what took me an hour. Learning from it is useful, but I can see where this goes if my job is the minute and not the hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas, or to your father, if they asked whether it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas to join the union and tell my father to look at AI tools to save time on quotes. I'd be honest with both of them: it's real, it's slower than the headlines, and the answer is to organise as well as adapt.

say: I'd bring a **union** motion for shared benefits like retraining funds and shorter hours.
I'd say firms that save the most from AI should pay a **tax**.
think: My economics degree sits in the zone AI touches: analysis, reports and **summaries**.
Entry-level analyst jobs are exactly what firms will cut **first**.
do: Learn to use AI tools **properly** so I can check what they produce.
Choose politics and policy modules and apply to two **internships** a term.
feel: **Anxious**, not panicking, because my future job could shrink.
S1.quote: I used a tool to debug my code last week and it did in a minute what took me an hour.
fieldNote: He knows from daily use how good the tools are, so his fear is informed.
His answer combines personal adaptation with **collective** action through the union.
He would advise his father on AI tools but not push it too hard.

steps.text: Take a short course on using AI for data analysis
Bring a union motion on retraining funds to the next meeting
Write to the economics faculty asking for policy modules
Switch two optional modules to public policy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to act, not argue. It's an emergency, and governments must slow it down or put a public stake in it. I'd say it to friends, I'd go on a demonstration, and I'd write to my local politician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think everything I'm studying could become pointless. If AI can do the thinking, what's the point of an economics degree? And the economy itself would be a mess: if lots of people lose income at once, nobody can buy anything, including the products firms make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the first year and keep the cafe shifts, because tips are money. I'd put every spare euro into savings and ask my parents to do the same. I'd join the union campaign for a universal basic income, and I'd learn how to build with AI tools so I'm useful in whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd probably be awake at night, running through what my parents will do if the print shop closes and my mum's school uses robots in the classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years leaves almost no room. How does your politics change when there is no time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop would struggle as customers move to AI design tools and online printing. My parents have savings, but not many, and my mum's pension is tied to her job. I'd have to be a bit of a safety net for them and I'm not sure I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your father's shop and your parents' savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, my politics gets sharper and less patient. I'd push for rules and public ownership because slow reform won't work in time. I'd put the blame on firms and governments that chose speed over safety.

say: I'd say it's an **emergency** and governments must slow AI down or take a public stake.
I'd join a demonstration and write to my local **politician**.
think: If AI does the thinking, my degree could become **pointless**.
A sudden loss of income across the economy means nobody can **buy** what firms make.
do: Put every spare euro into **savings** and keep the cafe shifts for tips.
Join the union campaign for a **basic income** and learn to build with AI tools.
feel: **Alarmed**, awake at night about my parents' print shop and my own degree.
S2.quote: If lots of people lose income at once, nobody can buy anything, including the products firms make.
fieldNote: He turns to **emergency** politics when time is short, and gets more impatient.
He links his father's shop and mother's school job to the wider economy.
He is already thinking of himself as a safety net for his parents.

steps.text: Save every spare euro from cafe tips for my parents
Write to my local politician about a public stake
Join the union campaign for a basic income
Build one small project with AI tools to learn them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a window and we should not waste it. Five years is enough to pass laws, set up retraining funds and decide who owns the technology. I'd say this on campus and in the union, and push the university to teach students how to use AI well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel a bit more hopeful. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years to find work before the big change, which is just about workable. But I also know I'm one of the people the thinking-AI hits first, so I'd keep a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and pick up a skill that connects people, like policy or consulting for small firms, where a human matters. I'd keep working part-time and save about 40 a week. I'd also help my dad move some of his print work online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which makes a big difference. Five years lets me feel I'm steering, not just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: would you still finish the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd finish it. A degree is still a signal, and the topics I'm learning matter for the rules. I'd just treat it as a base to build on, not as a ticket to a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd panic and push for emergency measures. With five years, I'd do a mix: finish the degree, help my dad, and press for laws. It's less angry, more organised.

say: I'd say we have a **window** to pass laws and set up retraining funds.
I'd ask the university to teach students how to use AI **well**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with about two years before the **big change**.
Thinking-AI hits people like me first, so I'd keep a **plan B**.
do: Finish the degree and add a people-facing skill like **policy** or small-firm consulting.
Save 40 a week and help my dad move print work **online**.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, feeling like I'm steering.
S3.quote: A degree is still a signal, and the topics I'm learning matter for the rules.
fieldNote: He treats the degree as a **base** and not a guaranteed ticket.
Five years moves him from emergency mode to a mixed plan.
Plan B is people-facing work, which suggests he sees humans staying valuable in advice.

steps.text: Finish the economics degree with a policy focus
Save 40 a week from cafe wages
Take a consulting course for small firms in second year
Help my dad put his print orders online this summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we can shape this. I'd push for a public fund, a shorter working week and strong rules on who owns the models. I'd be a bit more relaxed with friends, and point out we've handled big shifts before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly calm. I'd be 28, with several years in a job or maybe a master's. The danger is that people put it off and then the final years are chaos, so I'd still push for planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study as planned, do a master's in public policy, and work for a think tank or a union. I'd use AI tools in my work all the time by then, as everyone would. I'd keep saving small amounts and stay on the union committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A decade is long enough for me to build a career and still have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, does your view of the degree change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A public fund that pays people while they retrain, a shorter working week, and strong public control of the main AI systems. If those happen, then I'd be less scared even for my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want governments to have done by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it written down and passed in law, not promised. Ten years sounds generous, but politicians love to wait until the last minute. I'd work in politics partly to stop that happening.

say: I'd point out we've handled **big shifts** before and we can shape this one.
I'd push for a public fund and a shorter **working week**.
think: I'm fairly calm, but people put it off and the final years get **chaotic**.
I'd be 28 with years in a job or a **master's**.
do: Study as planned, then do a **master's** in public policy.
Work for a think tank or union and stay on the **union** committee.
feel: Mostly **calm**, since a decade is long enough to build a career.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds generous, but politicians love to wait until the last minute.
fieldNote: His calm is conditional on **laws** being passed, not promised.
He sees his own future in policy work, partly to stop delay.
Even with a decade, he is more worried about politicians than the technology.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply for a public policy master's
Stay on the student union committee through second year
Keep saving small amounts from cafe wages each week
Use AI tools every day in coursework as everyone will

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because everything I'm studying is meant to explain the economy and it might stop working. What would help is public money for retraining, and a way to keep a decent income while you retrain. Not a charity, a right.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether we trust the people running this. I do use these tools now and then, for summaries and for checking my statistics code, but using something doesn't mean I trust whoever owns it. I'd say we should treat AI like electricity: useful, and too important to leave to private owners.

headlineQuote: I'd say we should treat AI like electricity: useful, and too important to leave to private owners.
portrait: Umar is an 18-year-old **economics and politics** student who waits tables twice a week and sits on the student union committee.
His parents, a print-shop owner and a teacher, pay his rent; he covers food and transport himself.
He uses AI tools now and then, but wants **public ownership** and strong rules, and blames firms rather than workers.
He moves from uneasy to alarmed as the warning shrinks, worrying about his **father's print shop** as much as his own job.
He tends to act through the union and politics first, and only then adjusts his own plans.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, since it could undermine the whole economy he is studying and his father's shop.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **public money** for retraining and a guaranteed income while retraining, as a right and not charity.
